candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.98 malware probability, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking (SHAP +0.0049 to +0.0096). No benign-leaning features appear in the evidence. The strongest signals come from two families. The first is SIMD vector-register manipulation: PXOR MOVAPS (+0.009625), PXOR PXOR (+0.007721), MOVDQA MOVAPS (+0.007424), MOVDQA PAND (+0.006424), VPXOR VMOVDQU (+0.006396), PXOR MOVUPS (+0.005864) and PADDQ MOVDQA (+0.004933). These suggest vectorized XOR, AND and add operations on 128/256-bit data, which fits hashing or cipher inner loops such as those in proof-of-work mining algorithms. The second is rotate and shift arithmetic: ADD ROR (+0.009514), MOV ROL (+0.007223), ROL ADD (+0.006427), MOVZX ROL (+0.006385), ROL MOV (+0.005147), ADD ROL (+0.005063), SHL NEG (+0.006641) and SHRD SHR (+0.005894). Dense rotate/add/xor interleaving is typical of hash round functions, and SHRD/SHR points to multi-word big-integer shifting. Weaker, more generic sequences (POP SUB, SUB ADC, CALL PUSH, ADD PUSH, SUB CMOVG) also contribute positively. SUB ADC suggests multi-precision carry arithmetic, though the others are less specific on their own. The evidence lacks function-level locations, so it cannot show where these patterns occur or how they connect to each other. The conclusion rests on the combined n-gram profile, which is consistent with a compute-intensive hashing kernel, plus the very high model probability. It does not show actual mining behavior, since no network, pool or process-level evidence is provided. Heavy crypto/hash routines can also appear in legitimate software, so the call is made from the aggregate pattern, not any single n-gram.
